1:
The chapter opens as a court. Henry has the summons going out to the remotest islands, which are distant but not outside the jurisdiction of one who owns the ends of the earth, and silence proclaimed while the cause is heard; his advice is that onlookers watching the kingdom of God contend with the kingdom of Satan should keep quiet and expect the verdict rather than object to the proceedings. Wesley glosses the islands as the Gentile lands beyond the sea and reads the invitation as leave to say whatever can be said. Ellicott hears irony in the call to renew strength, since the challengers will need every reserve, and pictures the speaker as seeing, like the seer hired to curse, the far future opening and a new conqueror walking into it.

Keil and Delitzsch state the argument the court is to settle. The raising up of the conqueror is claimed as the work of the God exalted above the idols, and the claim is proved by what that career does: destruction for the idolatrous nations and the long-awaited release for God's people. They add the condition on which the reasoning depends — the conqueror must already be under way, since an event still unfulfilled would carry no force as present evidence.

Calvin turns the challenge inward. If pleading with blind unbelievers would have succeeded, the sluggishness of a people who had God so near them in the law is the more shameful. He then excuses them a little, on the ground that human nature carries two complementary diseases: in prosperity a man throws off restraint, and in adversity he either rages or lies down insensible, so that terror can leave even the well-taught unable to take hold of comfort.

Who the man from the east is divides the chapter's readers evenly. Gill takes him for Abraham and marshals the fit — called out of an idolatrous family beyond the river, obedient at once, given a land held by nations, made the father of many nations, victorious over kings — and reports the Jewish authorities behind that reading. Clarke agrees, arguing that the character of righteousness suits the patriarch better, and that the alarm of the idol-makers follows naturally on the entry of his posterity into a land they were sent to clear. Calvin chooses Abraham for a pastoral reason: exiles who found return incredible are pointed to an ancestor brought out of the same country through worse dangers, by a power not since diminished nor a kindness since cooled.

The other side is equally firm. Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley both name Cyrus, Wesley adding that Persia lies due east of Judea and of Babylon alike and that the prophet speaks of what is future as though past. Ellicott renders the clause as the man whom Righteousness calls to tread in his steps, insists the figure is the coming restorer, points to the same idea running through the neighbouring chapters, compares the earlier prophet's calling a pagan king the servant of the Lord, and mentions the patriarchal reading only in order to reject it. He also prefers a present tense throughout, the future seen as happening, and notes a variant that makes the sword itself the stubble.

The untrodden road at the end draws comment from both camps. Ellicott takes it for a new path and recalls how Assyrian kings boast in their inscriptions of leading armies where none had gone. Keil and Delitzsch read the march as unhindered, nobody able to touch him on a route he had never walked. Calvin makes the same fact evidence of help, since pursuing an enemy through unknown country is the hardest thing in war, as every soldier knows and every history shows. Clarke, characteristically, stops on a missing preposition that the old versions and one manuscript appear to have read.
4:
The question that answers itself is read for its verbs and its formula. Keil and Delitzsch separate the two words as bringing about and carrying out, so that the author is claimed for both the origin and the progress of the thing; and the one who has done it is the one who has been calling generations into being ever since there was human history. Gill says the same more briefly, that the scheme was contrived and then effected. Ellicott hears in the closing words the central thought of the nation's creed, the same declaration of eternal being that returns several times in these chapters and reappears at the end of the Bible as first and last. Wesley makes the calling a summoning out of nothing. Clarke notes that a word has dropped from the text, supplied by an old manuscript and by all the versions.

Calvin widens the appeal deliberately. Only one ancestor has been named, but the question is not about a single act: the people are to recall where they came from, by what road their father was led, and that the kindness did not stop with him but ran on through a succession of ages, which is what the word for generation carries. The argument is cumulative rather than anecdotal.

What the islands saw divides the readers again. Keil and Delitzsch take the trembling as the effect the conqueror's course had already begun to have on the heathen world, and note that the Hebrew pairs seeing and fearing by sound. Ellicott agrees on the cause but presses what the fear produced: not recognition of the Eternal but a rush to the shrines, each nation turning to its own oracle as sailors in a storm each call on their own god, with new statues commissioned and idol-making given fresh impetus, probably for images to carry into battle. Wesley has the remote countries afraid of being caught in the same calamity. Gill declines the whole conquest reading and applies the verse instead to the spread of the Gospel, with temples abandoned, idols neglected, and a particular panic among priests whose living depended on the old religion.

Calvin fixes on the ingratitude. A world that had seen enough to shudder went straight back to what it was, which leaves the most distant nations with no plea of ignorance, since the majesty on display was plain to anyone who had not shut his eyes on purpose. He then makes the mutual encouragement worse than the fear: they gathered not to consider but to league together and hearten one another in the manufacture of new gods, and he generalises from it that superstition always begins in men agreeing with each other to darken a light that came from above.

The workshop closes the passage. Gill has the wooden figure finished and the goldsmith hurried into plating it. Ellicott corrects the trade, reading caster rather than carpenter since the image is metal, and traces the sequence — plates laid on the anvil, smoothed with the hammer, the soldering pronounced good — before the last stroke of irony, the guardian god nailed down so that it will not fall over. Wesley has it fastened to a wall or pillar. Calvin admits the verse is obscure and that the Jewish authorities disagree, and works from the words themselves: the first names any craftsman, used elsewhere of workers in iron, wood, stone and brass, while the second is precise, one who melts metal, purges it of dross and separates one from another.
8:
Ellicott marks this as the first appearance of a figure who dominates the rest of the book. The servant, he says, is an idea of calling and election held in three concentric circles: the nation as it stands, the true nation realising its ideal, and innermost a single person who gathers the ideal into himself; he lines the three up with an apostle's distinction between the seed after the flesh, the heirs of the patriarch's faith, and the one seed who is Christ, and with the later distinction between a visible church falling short, a spiritual church approaching the mark, and Christ identified with his people. Here, he adds, it is the national sense that is in view.

Calvin takes the same election as a restraint. The unreasonable thing would be to confound this people with the nations, since a calling of free grace had set them apart, and a corrupted world is no licence: we are not at liberty to run past bounds as though we had never been chosen, and nothing is more absurd than to walk like blind men once the sun has risen on us. Gill reads the servant as the spiritual Israel rather than the natural, men turned from idols to the living God, and hears the comfort addressed to believers about to be persecuted.

Where the servant was fetched from is disputed in one clause. Ellicott identifies the ends of the earth with the city on the Euphrates that lay at the far edge of the prophet's horizon, and corrects the second phrase from the chief men to the far-off regions; Clarke reaches the same correction by another route, showing that the word means an arm or extremity and that it answers in parallel to the ends in the previous line. Wesley keeps the traditional sense, a man called out from among the great persons he lived among. Calvin allows two possibilities, either that the ancestor was brought from a remote country or that a God whose dominion reaches the world's edges stretched out his hand to one people only.

Ellicott makes the election preach. He calls the prophet its herald, finds in it the ground of an unquenchable hope for his own nation, and balances it against the apostolic charge to make one's calling sure, so that a choice made before the foundation of the world still leaves something to be done. Calvin notes the movement from one man to a whole people, and reads the relative clause as giving a reason: past kindness experienced is why courage is owed in present adversity.

Keil and Delitzsch turn the exclamation forward. The eye is directed to an intervention close at hand, in which the men of the quarrel come to nothing and are sought for without being found.

The command not to fear is handled tenderly by all of them. Henry observes that the words are addressed to the nation as to a single person, so that any individual can take them to himself, notes how often they are repeated, and concludes that it is against the mind of God that his people should be a timorous people. Gill distinguishes three ways of being present — by essence, by providence, and by special grace — and insists the third is meant. Ellicott finds in the verb for strengthening a second sense of attaching to oneself. Calvin is the most careful: the promise does not make believers so bold as to feel no fear at all, but distressed and tempted men resist steadily enough to win, and the natural timidity that tosses us about whenever we suspect God is absent is corrected by this reflection and no other. Clarke, as usual, records a conjunction added by many manuscripts which completes the sense.
11:
Calvin explains why the enemies are named at all. A bare promise of safety would leave the anxious wondering why adversaries still flourish, so the promise carries a circumstance: they prosper now and will be driven off ashamed. He distinguishes two sorts, those who use violence and those who use words, tearing men with slander and hauling them into court as though defending a good cause; and since routed enemies are not looked for, he reads the clause about seeking them as a consequence. Wesley states the reversal plainly, the mischief falling on its contrivers; Keil and Delitzsch note the encouragement repeated to promise not survival only but the upper hand.

The held hand is read for warmth. Gill hears a league entered and a walk hand in hand, and compares a child held by a parent and so afraid of nothing. Calvin defends the repetition, since a doctrine this hard to root slips out of mind however often said. Wesley reduces it to enablement against enemies.

The worm is where all of them stop. Gill and Clarke both report the rabbinic observation that a worm's strength lies in its soft mouth, which yet bores through the hardest cedar, and Clarke draws the application, that this people's strength is prayer, by which they cut down the mighty. Ellicott takes it as a reminder of having no strength at all, a nation chosen when it was fewest of peoples, and notices the shift from masculine to feminine here and back when strength given from outside is named. Calvin defends the apparent insult: to address men in deep wretchedness as an elect nation and royal priesthood would have been absurd, whereas naming the condition both laments and consoles.

The threshing sledge is described from life. Gill has corn crushed under a wheeled cart spiked with iron or a weighted drag toothed beneath; Clarke calls it a corn-drag and passes on the reading that makes the mountains the princes of the nations, which Wesley shares; Ellicott identifies a revolving sledge with two-edged blades still used in Syria, a standing figure for crushing victory. Calvin presses the reversal, a people nearly ground to powder given strength to grind, without which they would have stayed at anyone's mercy. On the winnowing, Gill recalls threshing floors set on hilltops to catch the wind, and Calvin distinguishes two kinds of bruising: the faithful are broken to their good, submitting to authority, while the obstinate are blown away.

Thirst is taken spiritually by most. Gill applies the want to believers lacking nothing in Christ and much in themselves; Ellicott lets the promise start from the help given returning exiles but says it rises into poetry where earthly things are parables of heavenly, needing no literal fulfilment. Calvin keeps it concrete, a preparation for extreme poverty in exile, thirst being chosen because nothing distresses men more.

The remedy runs to extravagance. Gill has nature's course changed rather than the people want; Wesley notes that mountains bear no rivers; Ellicott admires the varied iteration, every contour given the water that suits it; Calvin draws the lesson that God keeps secret methods in reserve, and that we despair because we will not hope beyond the aids we see. Clarke reads the planting as shade for travellers fainting in a hot land, citing a later book that uses the same image of the return. Ellicott sees a paradise of stately groves, wonders whether four and three making seven is deliberate, and names the species; Wesley admits the words cannot now be identified. On the purpose, Ellicott says the gifts should make men acknowledge the giver, Gill limits the seeing to the needy, Calvin observes that we are too sluggish to read God's works unprompted, and Clarke argues that a word for heart has dropped out, since every ancient version translates as though it stood there.
21:
The court reconvenes. Henry has the idols summoned to make their best case, and observes that nothing exposes an absurdity so well as letting its defenders state their reasons; a god must show understanding and active power, both in perfection. Clarke prefers a rendering calling the images forward as the mighty powers their owners think them. Ellicott sees the opening scene repeated, worshippers hurrying between oracles, and cites the Greek historian's picture of kings and cities consulting shrines about the new conqueror; the phrase for strong reasons is literally strongholds. Calvin adds the pastoral point: exiles hear their hope mocked as credulity, so the challenge arms them, God appearing as advocate for his church.

The test is prediction. Ellicott argues that the former things are not the remote past but the head of what is coming, so the question is whether these gods can see a year ahead as pledge for seeing further; the challenge matches the prophet's habit of offering signs, though some critics keep the other sense. Wesley reads it as things shortly to come, the latter end as whether events answer the forecast; Keil and Delitzsch note that the floor was given to the idols and nothing said.

The second demand is for any effect. Ellicott compares the taunt on Carmel and asks whether the nations can name one fortune, good or bad, that some deity announced beforehand and could therefore claim; every worshipper credits his god with blessings, but only prediction proves it. Calvin heads off a misreading of the word for evil: not injustice, which is against the divine nature, but adversity, which providence owns and neither idols nor fortune can. Wesley turns it into a dare: protect your own and destroy his.

The verdict is nothing, and they press what that means. Gill grants the material is gold or brass and denies only the divinity, reporting a rendering of less than nothing. Calvin makes the same distinction: quality is denied, not substance, since nobody adores metal as metal but the divinity imagined in it. Ellicott calls this the summing up in the Judge's name, and remarks that the apostolic account of heathen gods as demonic does not appear beside the account of them as nothing. Wesley matches operations to beings. Clarke argues from the versions that a letter is corrupted, while noting that the rabbis deny any error and treat the two forms as one.

Who comes from the north is the second great dispute. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch divide the compass between Media and Persia and make both one conqueror, Ellicott adding that the verb allows invoking or proclaiming the name, fulfilled in the decree, and that the word for princes is a borrowed title for a satrap. Wesley agrees, explaining the northern direction by a Median mother, contingent and colleague. Gill offers the same, and preserves the alternative that two men are meant. Calvin takes that alternative, making the north the Babylonians and the east the Medes and Persians, two revolutions worth remembering. Clarke reports two further readings, one making the figure the Messiah, the other applying the chapter to the patriarch because the tenses are past.

The close returns to knowledge. Keil and Delitzsch note that the argument answers its two earlier charges in turn, ruler and then omniscient. Ellicott says no oracle in Assyria, Babylon or the Phoenician coasts anticipated its suddenness. Calvin hears a taunt, a promise to acknowledge as true God whoever can do the like, and notes that the word rendered righteous can mean approved. On the herald, Clarke paraphrases a transposed sentence into one announcement; Ellicott gives two renderings and thinks the messenger reports the victories rather than being the conqueror. Calvin insists prophecy exists to build up the church, not to inform. Wesley closes on the words for wind and confusion, the second being the term for the rude heap before creation.
